author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: ah
fields.label: Battery capacity
fields.hint: 150 Ah and 200 Ah are the common Pakistani tubular sizes. Enter the Ah of one battery, not the total of a bank.

fields.name: load_w
fields.label: Load
fields.hint: Total watts on backup. A ceiling fan is under a hundred watts; a fridge, TV and several fans together are a few hundred.

fields.name: inverter_eff
fields.label: Inverter efficiency
fields.hint: As a decimal. A basic home UPS is about 0.85; a good hybrid inverter about 0.9.

fields.name: dod
fields.label: Usable depth of discharge
fields.hint: As a decimal: 0.5 means half the battery. Leave blank to use the value for your battery type.

answer: A {{in.ah|int}} Ah, {{in.volts|int}} V tubular battery gives about {{out.hours|hm}} of backup for a {{in.load_w|int}} W load (a fan, lights and a TV) through a home UPS, using the safe {{out.dod|pct}} of its capacity. Backup hours = Ah × volts × usable depth of discharge × inverter efficiency ÷ load watts; the chart below shows common loads.
how: {{in.ah|int}} Ah × {{in.volts|1}} V × {{out.dod|pct}} usable × {{out.inverter_eff|pct}} inverter efficiency = {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh usable. {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh ÷ {{in.load_w|int}} W = {{out.hours|2}} hours, about {{out.hours|hm}}.
key_facts: A {{in.ah|int}} Ah, {{in.volts|int}} V tubular battery stores about {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh of usable energy for a UPS when used to the recommended {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} of its rating.

That {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh runs one ceiling fan ({{ex.0.in.load_w|int}} W) for about {{ex.0.out.hours|hm}}, two fans with lights ({{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W) for about {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}}, and a {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W load for only about {{ex.2.out.hours|hm}}.

A {{ex.3.in.ah|int}} Ah lithium (LiFePO4) battery at {{ex.3.in.volts|1}} V gives about {{ex.3.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.3.in.load_w|int}} W, almost twice the tubular figure, because it can use about {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}} of its capacity.
A {{ex.4.in.ah|int}} Ah tubular battery gives three quarters of the backup of a {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery at the same load: about {{ex.4.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.4.in.load_w|int}} W.

lines: Ah = battery capacity in amp hours

sections.h2: How to read the {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery backup chart
p: The chart below uses the loads most Pakistani homes put on a UPS. One ceiling fan is about {{ex.0.in.load_w|int}} W; two fans with LED lights about {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W; a fan, lights and a TV about {{in.load_w|int}} W; a fridge with fans a few hundred watts more; and {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W is the kind of load an iron, a microwave or a water motor adds. Each row is a {{in.volts|int}} V tubular battery through a UPS at about {{d.inverter_eff_ups|pct}} efficiency, using {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} of the battery.

Every doubling of the load halves the backup. To stretch a {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery through a long outage, keep the TV and fridge off the UPS and run only fans and lights; the backup climbs from about {{out.hours|hm}} to about {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}}.

A {{ex.4.in.ah|int}} Ah tubular battery at {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V holds about {{ex.4.out.usable_wh|int}} Wh of usable energy through a UPS. That is about {{ex.4.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.4.in.load_w|int}} W (two fans and lights); at {{in.load_w|int}} W with a TV added it drops to about three quarters of the {{in.ah|int}} Ah figure of {{out.hours|hm}}. The {{ex.4.in.ah|int}} Ah rows in the chart give the exact hours for each load.

If a {{ex.4.in.ah|int}} Ah battery is not enough, a second battery in series on a {{d.battery_v_default|int}} V UPS doubles the energy, but you must change the bank voltage to {{d.battery_v_default|int}} V in the calculator rather than entering the Ah twice.

examples.text: One ceiling fan at {{in.load_w|int}} W: {{in.ah|int}} Ah × {{in.volts|int}} V × {{out.dod|pct}} × {{out.inverter_eff|pct}} = {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh, ÷ {{in.load_w|int}} W = about {{out.hours|hm}}, a whole night.

examples.title: {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery for two fans and lights
examples.text: Two fans with a few LED bulbs are about {{in.load_w|int}} W. {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh ÷ {{in.load_w|int}} W = about {{out.hours|hm}} on a {{in.volts|int}} V tubular battery.

examples.title: {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery for a {{in.load_w|int}} W load
examples.text: {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh ÷ {{in.load_w|int}} W = about {{out.hours|hm}}. The UPS draws about a hundred amps from the battery at this load, and a tubular battery drained this fast gives less than its label Ah, so the real figure is shorter.

examples.text: {{in.ah|int}} Ah × {{in.volts|1}} V × {{out.dod|pct}} × {{out.inverter_eff|pct}} = {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh usable. At {{in.load_w|int}} W that is about {{out.hours|hm}}, roughly double the tubular figure for the same load in the chart.

mistakes: Counting the full {{in.ah|int}} Ah. A tubular battery should only be taken to about {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}}; going deeper every day cuts its life to a year or two.
Entering the Ah of two batteries added together. Two batteries in series on a {{d.battery_v_default|int}} V UPS keep the same Ah and double the volts; set the bank voltage instead.
Forgetting the inverter loss. The UPS turns only about {{d.inverter_eff_ups|pct}} of the battery energy into AC power.
Expecting the chart figure at a {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W load. The label Ah is rated over about twenty hours; drained in an hour a tubular battery gives noticeably less.
safety: Keep tubular batteries in a ventilated place away from sparks, use cables and fuses rated for the UPS current, and have a licensed electrician connect the UPS to house wiring.

faq.q: What is the {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery backup time for one fan?
faq.a: About {{ex.0.out.hours|hm}} for one ceiling fan of about {{ex.0.in.load_w|int}} W on a {{in.volts|int}} V tubular battery through a UPS. An inverter fan or a DC fan draws less and runs longer.

faq.q: A {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery gives how many hours?
faq.a: About {{out.hours|hm}} at {{in.load_w|int}} W, about {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W and about {{ex.0.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.0.in.load_w|int}} W. The usable energy is fixed at about {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh; the hours depend on the load.

faq.q: How much backup does a {{in.ah|int}} Ah tubular battery give?
faq.a: The calculator uses {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} of the rating and a UPS at about {{d.inverter_eff_ups|pct}} efficiency, giving about {{out.usable_wh|int}} Wh and {{out.hours|hm}} at {{in.load_w|int}} W. Many UPS units run the battery lower than that, which gives more hours but a shorter battery life.

faq.q: What is the backup of a {{in.ah|int}} Ah lithium battery?
faq.a: About {{ex.3.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.3.in.load_w|int}} W for a {{ex.3.in.volts|1}} V LiFePO4 battery, nearly double the tubular figure, because lithium can use about {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}} of its capacity. Switch the battery type to lithium above to see other loads.

faq.q: Can a {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery run a {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W load?
faq.a: Only for about {{ex.2.out.hours|hm}}, and less in practice because of the fast-discharge drop. The UPS must also be rated for {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W or more; a typical home UPS of about a kVA cannot deliver it.

faq.q: Is there an inverter battery {{in.ah|int}} Ah backup chart?
faq.a: Yes, the chart above lists one fan, two fans with lights, fan with lights and TV, fridge with fans and a {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W load for {{in.ah|int}} Ah and {{ex.4.in.ah|int}} Ah tubular batteries. Change the inputs for any other combination.

faq.q: How long does a {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery run two fans and lights?
faq.a: About {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}} for a {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W load on a {{in.volts|int}} V tubular battery, which covers an evening of loadshedding with margin to spare.

faq.q: What is the backup time of a {{ex.4.in.ah|int}} Ah battery?
faq.a: About {{ex.4.out.hours|hm}} for two fans and lights ({{ex.4.in.load_w|int}} W), from about {{ex.4.out.usable_wh|int}} Wh usable. For a fan, lights and TV expect three quarters of the {{out.hours|hm}} that a {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery gives.
